assessment.Applicability of Article 10: The applicant’s conduct falls within the scope of Article 10 as the wearing of a plastic visor with the inscription “smash capitalism” during a demonstration constituted an expression of a political opinion (see paragraph 6). The European Court of Human Rights (“the Court”) has consistently held that freedom of expression extends to the display of symbols and messages in a public context, including during protests (see no. 26986/03).

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant’s conviction for carrying a protective weapon under sections 17a(1) and 27(2) § 1 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions, which resulted in a criminal penalty (see paragraphs 8-15), amounts to an interference with his right to freedom of expression as guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention.

assessment.Prescribed by law and legitimate aim: The interference was based on sections 17a(1) and 27 of the Act on Public Assemblies and Processions, thus satisfying the requirement that it be “prescribed by law” (see paragraphs 17-18). The measure pursued the legitimate aims of preventing disorder and protecting the rights of others, as it was intended to prevent the use of protective weapons which could escalate tensions at public assemblies (see paragraph 19).

assessment.Necessity in a democratic society: However, the interference was not necessary in a democratic society. First, the demonstration in which the applicant participated was peaceful and organised under the slogan “colourful, loud – but peaceful” (see paragraph 6). The applicant’s group was distinct from the violent groups described in paragraph 7, which were acting separately in the same district. The domestic courts failed to differentiate between the applicant’s peaceful conduct and the violent actions of others. The Court has held that restrictions on protest-related expression must be based on the specific conduct of the individual concerned and not on general risks (see no. 20652/92). Furthermore, the plastic visor had a clear expressive purpose, as it bore a political slogan. The domestic courts acknowledged the inscription but dismissed its relevance, stating that the visor’s primary purpose was protective (see paragraphs 11 and 13). However, the Court has recognised that objects can have dual purposes, and where they convey a message, their restriction must be justified by reference to that expression. In particular, the display of political slogans during protests is entitled to strong protection under Article 10 (see no. 26986/03). The fact that the police did not intervene during the demonstration (see paragraph 6) suggests that the applicant’s conduct was not perceived as an immediate threat to public order at the time. Additionally, less restrictive measures, such as a request to remove the visor, could have been considered before resorting to a criminal conviction. The severity of the penalty imposed on the applicant—initially 60 daily rates at EUR 30 each (see paragraph 9)—further underscores the disproportionate nature of the interference.

assessment.Conclusion: Given that the restriction was not proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and failed to account for the expressive nature of the applicant’s conduct in the context of a peaceful protest, the conviction amounted to a violation of Article 10 of the Convention. The Court has previously found violations in cases where domestic authorities imposed restrictions on protest-related expression without demonstrating that such measures were necessary and proportionate (see no. 31684/05).
